title: Wait Queue
explain: A wait queue is the holding area for work that cannot run yet: waiting for a worker, a lock, a rate-limit token, a dependency or a scheduled time. It does not add capacity; it turns a temporary excess of demand into waiting time. So the real design questions are how long, how many, in what order, and what happens to items that waited too long.
model:
Knobs of a wait queue:

```
arrivals --> [ bounded queue, each item has a deadline ] --> worker slot frees --> check deadline --> run / drop
               full? reject immediately (503)
```

- **Size.** Wait for a newcomer is about `queue length / service rate` (Little's law). At 100 tasks/s, 600 queued means 6 s. If callers give up after 2 s, anything past 200 is doomed, so **bound the queue** and reject or shed the excess ([load shedding](#/sd/f/load-shedding), [concurrency limiter](#/sd/f/concurrency-limiter)).
- **Order.** FIFO is fair; a priority queue serves important work first but needs aging ([prioritized scheduling](#/sd/f/prioritized-scheduling)); under overload with deadlines, **LIFO** answers the most requests in time.
- **Staleness.** Store the deadline; check at dequeue; drop expired items.
- **Blocking vs async.** A thread per waiter is expensive; a queue of callbacks is cheap.
- **Visibility.** Alert on queue age, not just length.

Variants: delay queues hold items until a due time ([trigger-based invocation](#/sd/f/trigger-based-invocation)); items moving into a running set is [wait / running queues](#/sd/f/wait-running-queues).

details.q: 100 tasks/s of capacity and callers abandon after 2 s. What is the longest useful queue?
details.a: 200 tasks: a newcomer behind 200 waits about 2 s. Beyond that it will be abandoned before it starts, so the work would be wasted. Bound the queue at roughly that length.

details.q: Arrivals are 120/s, capacity 100/s, unbounded FIFO. What happens?
details.a: The queue grows by 20 per second: after a minute 1,200 are waiting, a 12 s delay, and it keeps growing along with memory use. An unbounded queue under sustained overload only turns throughput loss into latency and eventual failure.

details.q: A worker dequeues a task whose caller deadline passed 3 s ago. What does it do?
details.a: Discard it, perhaps counting a metric. Nobody is waiting, and running it delays tasks that still matter. That is why the deadline travels with the item.

details.q: During a surge, requests have 1 s deadlines and the oldest queued items are 5 s old. Which order?
details.a: LIFO (newest first), at least while the queue is long, with expired items dropped. FIFO would serve only stale requests that have already timed out, answering almost nobody in time.

details.q: Why alert on queue age instead of length?
details.a: Length means different delays at different service rates; age is exactly what the next user will feel. A short queue of stuck items still has high age.

details.q: How do you implement waiting without a thread per waiter?
details.a: Enqueue a callback, promise or continuation and let a small worker pool drain the queue. Blocking threads costs stack memory and context switches and does not scale to thousands of waiters.

prompts.q: Explain what a wait queue is and what you must decide when designing one.
points: Holds work that cannot run yet
Turns excess demand into waiting time, not capacity
Bound the size, choose order, handle staleness

prompts.q: Use Little's law to size a queue for 100 tasks/s and 2 s caller timeout.
points: Wait is about length divided by service rate
Reject beyond it rather than queue doomed work
Check the deadline at dequeue as well

prompts.q: Compare FIFO, priority and LIFO ordering for a wait queue under overload.
points: Priority serves important work, needs aging
LIFO answers most requests within deadline under overload
